questions.question: Identify the hydrosphere: name its three states with a location for each, quote the two key proportions, and explain the difference between the hydrosphere and the water cycle.
questions.expected_answer: The hydrosphere is all the Earth's water. Liquid: oceans, rivers, lakes and groundwater soaked into rock. Frozen: polar ice sheets, glaciers, icebergs and permafrost. Vapour: the gas phase in the atmosphere. About 97% is salty ocean; the fresh, liquid, reachable water is well under 1% of the total. The hydrosphere is the STORE (the water itself, wherever it sits); the water cycle is the set of PROCESSES that move water between stores.

questions.question: Describe how building a dam affects people and ecology, giving at least two benefits and three costs, and name the investigation methods a scientist would use to study these effects.
questions.expected_answer: Benefits: stored wet-season water gives reliable drinking water and irrigation through dry seasons and droughts (e.g. Theewaterskloof for Cape Town, Katse for Gauteng), plus hydroelectric power at large dams. Costs: upstream flooding drowns farmland, homes and communities and forces relocation; downstream natural flood pulses stop, starving floodplains and disrupting fish spawning and bird breeding; the wall blocks fish migration; sediment is trapped, filling the reservoir while downstream lands lose fertile silt; still water favours weeds and mosquitoes. Methods: interview long-time residents from before and after the dam, consult literature about the region, and compare ecology upstream and downstream.

questions.question: A rural family draws cloudy borehole water. Describe how they could test it for dissolved ions and purify it, and state which contaminant no filter or boil can remove.
questions.expected_answer: Test pH first, then run the ion drill: dilute nitric acid (fizzing reveals carbonate), then silver nitrate (white = chloride, cream = bromide, yellow = iodide), then barium nitrate on a fresh acidified sample (persistent white = sulfate); test strips check nitrates/nitrites, which warn of fertiliser or sewage contamination, and a microscope reveals microorganisms. Purify in order: sedimentation (let grit settle), filtration (sand/gravel or filter paper traps fine particles), disinfection (chlorine, or boiling for a minute) because microbes pass every filter. Dissolved salts survive both filtration and boiling — removing them needs distillation/desalination.
